In the same vein. Judge Kavanaugh went on to question whether State Farm 
itself, or rather its pattern of apphcation by the lower courts, was consistent 
with the APA:
* * * [I]t bears repeating that § 553 of the APA requires only a notice
providing a “description of the subjects and issues involved”; time for 
interested persons to comment; and a “concise general statement” of 
the rule’s ‘hasis and purpose.” 5 U.S.C. § 553. Courts have 
incrementally expanded those APA procedural requirements well 
beyond what the text provides. And courts simultaneously have 
grown State Farm's 
§ 706 arbitrary-and-capricious review
into a far more demanding test. Apphcation of the beefed-up 
arbitrary-and-capricious test is inevitably if not inherently 
unpredictable—so much so that, on occasion, the courts’ arbitrary- 
and-capricious review itself appears arbitrary and capricious.
Over time, those twin hnes of decisions have gradually 
transformed rulemaking—^whether regulatory or deregulatory 
rulemaking—^from the simple and speedy practice contemplated by 
the APA into a laborious, seemingly never-ending process. The 
judicially created obstacle course can hinder Executive Branch 
agencies from rapidly and effectively responding to changing or 
emerging issues within their authority, such as consumer access to 
broadband, or effectuating pohcy or philosophical changes in the 
Executive’s approach to the subject matter at hand. * * *
In a response to critiques like those made by then-Judge Kavanaugh, 
Professor Ronald Levin acknowledges that courts have interpreted the APA in 
a relatively broad, evolving manner, adding that he has “no significant quarrel 
with” the several scholars who have used the label “administrative common 
law” to describe the judicial handiwork that is nominally interpretation of the 
APA. Levin cites examples of this judicial approach in several areas of 
administrative law, including informal rulemaking procedure, such as the 
Portland Cement demand for disclosure of studies, the Long Island Care 
requirement that a final rule be a ‘logical outgrowth” of an NPRM, the refusal 
in Auto Parts to take literally APA section 553’s description of the rulemaking 
preamble as “concise” (seemingly ratified in State Farm), and the demand that 
agencies respond to significant comments (articulated in cases like 
International Fabricare and arguably mandated by State Farm). Levin defends 
all these creative developments as pragmatic responses to agencies’ dramatic 
shift toward rulemaking in the 1960s and 1970s, fulfilhng the AiPAs general 
purposes of promoting fair and rational process under changed conditions. As 
to Vermont Yankee, Levin says:
